title: CAP Theorem
overview: The CAP Theorem (Brewer's Theorem) states that a distributed data store can guarantee at most two of three properties simultaneously: Consistency, Availability, and Partition Tolerance. Since network partitions are inevitable in real distributed systems, the real choice is between CP (consistency over availability) and AP (availability over consistency).
keyPoints: Consistency: Every read receives the most recent write or an error
Availability: Every request receives a non-error response (may be stale)
Partition Tolerance: System continues to operate despite network partitions
Network partitions are unavoidable — the real trade-off is C vs A
PACELC extends CAP: considers latency vs consistency trade-off even without partitions
Most systems allow tunable consistency levels (strong, eventual, bounded staleness)

concepts.name: CP Systems
concepts.description: Prioritize Consistency over Availability during partitions. Nodes may refuse requests to prevent returning stale data. Examples: HBase, ZooKeeper, etcd, MongoDB (default).

concepts.name: AP Systems
concepts.description: Prioritize Availability over Consistency during partitions. All nodes respond but may return stale data. Examples: Cassandra, CouchDB, DynamoDB. Use eventual consistency.

concepts.name: Eventual Consistency
concepts.description: Given no new updates, all replicas will eventually converge to the same value. The window of inconsistency is bounded. Acceptable for social feeds, shopping carts, DNS.

concepts.name: Strong Consistency
concepts.description: All nodes see the same data at the same time. Every read reflects the latest committed write. Requires synchronous replication or consensus (Raft, Paxos).

tools.name: Cassandra
tools.description: AP system with tunable consistency levels (ONE, QUORUM, ALL)

tools.name: ZooKeeper / etcd
tools.description: CP systems used for distributed coordination and configuration

tools.name: DynamoDB
tools.description: AP by default, offers optional strongly consistent reads at higher cost

tools.name: Spanner
tools.description: Google's globally distributed CP database using TrueTime for external consistency

tradeoffs: Choosing CP means some requests fail during partitions — acceptable for financial systems where stale data is costly. Choosing AP means requests always succeed but may serve stale data — acceptable for social media where consistency lag is tolerable. Most modern systems offer tunable consistency, allowing developers to choose per-operation.
interviewTips: Examiners love asking 'which databases are CP vs AP' — memorize a few examples for each
Always clarify that partition tolerance is non-negotiable in a real distributed system
Discuss PACELC as an extension — even without partitions, there's a latency vs consistency trade-off
Eventual consistency is often sufficient — explain how to design idempotent operations around it
